## [00:00] History of Neural Networks

**Spoken content:** Today, we'll talk about the history of neural networks from 1943 to the present day, 2019. Although the study of the human brain is thousands of years old, the first step towards neural networks took place in 1943.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline title: History of Neural Networks 1943-2019](video-frame://45@00:03)

## [00:15] 1943: McCulloch and Pitts

**Spoken content:** In 1943, Warren McCulloch, a neurophysiologist, and a young mathematician, Walter Pitts, wrote a paper on how neurons might work. They modeled a simple neural network with electrical circuits.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1943 Warren McCulloch & Walter Pitts wrote a paper on how neurons might work; they modeled a simple neural network with electrical circuits.](video-frame://45@00:18)

## [00:31] 1949: Donald Hebb

**Spoken content:** In 1949, Donald Hebb reinforced the concept of neurons in his book, *The Organization of Behavior*. He pointed out that neural pathways are strengthened each time they are used.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1949 Donald Hebb reinforced the concept of neurons in his book, The Organization of Behavior. It pointed out that neural pathways are strengthened each time they are used.](video-frame://45@00:37)

## [00:46] 1950s: Nathaniel Rochester

**Spoken content:** In the 1950s, Nathaniel Rochester from the IBM Research Laboratories led the first effort to simulate a neural network.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1950s Nathaniel Rochester from the IBM Research Laboratories led the first effort to simulate a neural network.](video-frame://45@00:50)

## [00:57] 1956: Dartmouth Summer Research Project

**Spoken content:** In 1956, the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, or AI, provided a boost to both AI and neural networks. This stimulated research in AI and the much lower-level neural processing of the brain.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1956 The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence provided a boost to both Artificial Intelligence and Neural Networks.](video-frame://45@01:00)

## [01:15] 1957: John Von Neumann

**Spoken content:** In 1957, John Von Neumann suggested imitating simple neuron functions by using the telegraph relays or vacuum tubes.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1957 John Von Neumann suggested imitating simple neuron functions by using telegraph relays or vacuum tubes.](video-frame://45@01:20)

## [01:29] 1958: Frank Rosenblatt's Perceptron

**Spoken content:** Moving on to 1958, where Frank Rosenblatt, who was a neurobiologist, began work on the Perceptron. He was basically intrigued with the operation of the eye of a fly. Much of the processing which tells a fly to flee is done in its eye. The Perceptron, which resulted from this research, was built in hardware and is the oldest neural network still in use today. A single layer Perceptron was found to be useful in classifying a continuous valued set of inputs into one of the two classes. The Perceptron computes a weighted sum of the inputs, subtracts the threshold, and passes one of two possible values out as the result.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1958 Frank Rosenblatt began work on the Perceptron.](video-frame://45@01:33)

## [02:16] 1959: ADALINE and MADALINE

**Spoken content:** In 1959, Bernard Widrow and Marcian Hoff of Stanford developed models they called ADALINE and MADALINE. These models were named for their use of the multiple adaptive linear elements. MADALINE was actually the first neural network to be applied to a real-world problem. It's an adaptive filter which eliminates echoes on phone lines. This neural network is still in commercial use.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1959 Bernard Widrow & Marcian Hoff of Stanford developed models they called ADALINE and MADALINE to be applied to a real-world problem.](video-frame://45@02:20)

## [02:45] 1969: Minsky and Papert's Critique

**Spoken content:** In 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert proved that the Perceptron to be limited in their book *Perceptrons*. Progress on neural network research actually halted due to fear, unfulfilled claims, etc., until about 1981. This caused respected voices to critique the neural network research. The result was a halt to much of the funding, and this period of stunted growth lasted through 1981.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1969 Marvin Minsky & Seymour Papert proved the Perceptron to be limited in their book, Perceptrons.](video-frame://45@02:48)
![timeline event: 1982 Progress on neural network research halted due to fear, unfulfilled claims, etc. until 1981.](video-frame://45@02:56)

## [03:18] 1982: John Hopfield and US-Japan Conference

**Spoken content:** In 1982, John Hopfield presented a paper to the National Academy of Sciences. His approach to create useful devices was great, and he was basically likable, articulate, and charismatic. In 1982, additionally, the US-Japan Conference on Cooperative Competitive Neural Networks took place, at which Japan announced their fifth-generation effort, which resulted in the US really worrying about being left behind, and soon funding was flowing once again.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1982 John Hopfield presented a paper to the National Academy of Sciences. His approach to create useful devices, likable, articulate, and charismatic.](video-frame://45@03:20)
![timeline event: 1982 US-Japan Conference on Cooperative Competitive Neural Networks announced: Japan announced their fifth generation effort resulted in US worrying about being left behind and restarted the funding in US.](video-frame://45@03:34)

## [03:52] 1985 & 1987: Neural Networks for Computing and IEEE Conference

**Spoken content:** In 1985, the American Institute of Physics began what has become an annual meeting: Neural Networks for Computing. And by 1987, which was two years into it, the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineering (IEEE)'s first international conference on neural networks drew more than 1,800 attendees.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1985 American Institute of Physics began an annual meeting, Neural Networks for Computing.](video-frame://45@03:54)
![timeline event: 1987 IEEE's first International Conference on Neural Networks drew more than 1800 attendees.](video-frame://45@04:02)

## [04:17] 1997: LSTM

**Spoken content:** In 1997, a recurrent neural network framework, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), was proposed by Schimberger and Hochreiter.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1997 A recurrent neural network framework, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) was proposed by Schimber and Hochreiter.](video-frame://45@04:20)

## [04:30] 1998: Gradient-based Learning

**Spoken content:** In 1998, Yann LeCun published "Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition."

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: 1998 Yann LeCun published Gradient-based Learning applied to Document Recognition.](video-frame://45@04:32)

## [04:36] Now: The Future is Here

**Spoken content:** Several steps have actually taken place in order to get to where we are now. And today, neural networks are discussed really regularly, and the future is here. Currently, most neural network development is simply proving that the principle works. However, this research is developing neural networks that, due to processing limitations, take weeks to learn. But the future is here, and it's moving really quickly.

**On-screen content:**
![timeline event: NOW](video-frame://45@04:37)
